title: 5. Max Flow
content: # Lecture ## Setup - A directed graph $G = (V, E)$. - We have two special vertices $s$ (the source) and $t$ (the sink / target). - Every edge has a capacity $c: E \rightarrow N^+$. We want to send a "flow" from $s$ to $t$. - WLOG there are no anti-parallel edges A flow is a function $f: E \rightarrow R^+ \cup \{ 0 \}$ satisfying: - $\forall e \in E$, $f(e) \leq c(e)$ - The flow of a node can't be bigger than it's capacity - $\forall v \in V \backslash \{ s, t\}, f^{in}(v) = f^{out}(v)$ - The flow coming in must equal the flow coming out $⊽(f) = f^{out}(s)$ is the value of a flow. ### Useful Notation - $f^{in}(v) = \sum_{\text{ e going into v}} f(e)$ - $f^{out}(v) = \sum_{\text{ e going out of v}} f(e)$ - $f^{in}(S) = \sum_{v \in S} f^{in}(v)$ - $f^{out}(S) = \sum_{v \in S} f^{out}(v)$ ### Lemma 1 (for $\unicode{x22BD} f$) - For any flow $f$ we have $f^{out}(s) = f^{in}(t)$ Suppose that $\gamma$ is all nodes. THEN $$f^{in}(\gamma) = f^{in}(V \backslash \{ s \})$$ $$= f^{in}(t) + f^{in}(V \backslash \{ s, t \})$$ We can use this exact same strategy for $f^{out}$ and arrive at $f^{out}(\gamma) = f^{out}(s) + f^{out}(V \backslash \{ s, t\})$ Then we can substitute these expressions in $f^{out}(s) = f^{in}(t)$ and will arrive at 0 which proves the claim. ## The Problem Given the setup above, **Input**: A flow network $(G, c, s, t)$ **Output**: A flow $f:E \rightarrow R^+ \cup \{ 0 \}$ of value $\unicode{x22BD} (f) = v^*$ where $v^* = \max_{\text{flow f'}}\{ \unicode{x22BD}(f')\}$ ## The Naive Greedy Algorithm ### Idea Find a $s \rightarrow t$ path on which we can increase the flow, and increase the flow through it as much as we can. Repeat until there's no such path left. $$ \begin{aligned} &\textbf{Input: } G, c, s, t\\ &1.\ \text{let } f \equiv 0\\ &2.\ \text{while there is an } s \to t \text{ path } P \text{ such that } \forall e \in P,\ f(e) < c(e):\\ &\qquad \text{let } m = \min_{e \in P} \{c(e)-f(e)\}\\ &4.\ \text{for each } e \in P,\ \text{increase } f(e) \text{ by } m\\ &5.\ \text{return } f \end{aligned} $$ *This algorithm can make a "mistake" which it can't undo* ## Ford-Fulkerson **Idea** - Like the naive algo. but it allows us to correct our mistakes - At each iteration, we create an auxiliary graph that allows, at each edge, to either push more flow or "pushing flow back". - Map flows in the auxiliary graph to flows in the actual graph **Definition: Residual Network** Let $G = (V,E)$, and let $f$ be a flow. The *residual network* $G_f = ( V, E_f )$ with *capacity function* $c_f$ is defined as follows. For each $e = (u,v) \in E$: - If $f(u, v) < c(u, v)$, add $e$ to $E_f$ with $c_f(u, v) = c(u, v) - f(u, v)$ “forward” - If $f(u, v) > 0$: add the reserve of $e$ to $E_f$ with $c_f (v, u) = f(u, v)$ "backward" **Definition: Augmenting Path** Let $(G, c, s , t)$ be a flow network, let $f$ be a flow, let $G_f$ be the residual network. We say that a path $P$ in $G_f$ is an **augmenting path** if $P$ is a simple $s \rightarrow t$ path. - Recall that a simple path means that no vertex appears more than once **Definition: Augmenting a Flow** Let $(G, c, s , t)$ be a flow network, let $f$ be a flow, let $G_f$ be the residual network, and let $P$ be an augmenting path in $G_f$. The procedure of **augmenting $f$ by $P$** creates a new $f^+$ from $f$ as follows: For every $e' = (u, v) \in P$, - if $e'$ is a forward edge, then increase $f(u, v)$ by $m$ - if $e'$ is a backward edge, then decrease $f(v, u)$ by $m$ where $m = min_{e' \in P} \{ c_{f}(e') \}$ ### Proposition Let $(G,c,s,t)$ be a flow network, let $f$ be a flow, let $G_f$ be the residual network, let $P$ be an augmenting path in $G_f$. Let $f^+$ be obtained when augmenting $f$ by $P$. Then: 1. $f^+$ is a flow in $G$ 2. If $f$ had integer values, then $f^+$ has integer values and $⊽(f^+) \geq ⊽(f) + 1$ **Proof of 1.** We start by showing that $f^+$ is a flow in $G$. To do this we must show that: 1. $f^+$ respects capacity constraints: $\forall e \in E, f^+(e) \leq c(e)$ 2. $\forall v \in V \backslash \{ s, t \}, f^+_{out}(v) = f^+_{in}(v)$ $f^+$ respects capacity constraints because augmentation increases only by $m = min_{e' \in P} \{ c_{f}(e') \}$ where $c_f(e) = c(e) - f(e)$ for forward edges. Thus it must be the case that $f^+(e) \leq c(e)$ given that $f$ was a flow in $G$ As for 2. Let $v \in V \backslash \{ s, t\}$ be arbitrary. If $v \notin P$, it's flow has not been changed and the property holds trivially. Otherwise, since $P$ is a simple $s-t$ path in the residual network, we can say that for every vertex $v$ except $s,t$: - one edge enters $v$ - one edge leaves $v$ We have 4 cases: 1. ... **Proof of 2.** Suppose $f$ had integer values. It will immediately follow that $f^+$ is integer valued if we can show that $m \geq 1$ is an integer . Recall that $m = \min \{ c_f(e) \}$ and $c_f$ is defined as follows: - For forward edges, $c_f(e) = c(e) - f(e)$ - For backward edges, $c_f(e) = f(e)$ Since $c_f(e)$ is clearly positive it is clear that $m \geq 1$ Since $c$ and $f$ are integer valued, their addition and subtraction will also be integer valued. To show that $⊽(f^+) \geq ⊽(f) + 1$: The value changes according to the net flow out of s because s is the first vertex of the path, the path $P$ has an edge leaving $s$, but no edge entering $s$. Now check both possibilities for that first residual edge: - if it is a forward residual edge $(s,v)$, then $f(s,v)$ increases by $m$ - if it is a backward residual edge $(s,v)$, that means $(v,s)$ is an original edge and $f(v,s)$ decreases by $m$ ### Attempt 1: Pseudo-polynomial Time Impl. $$ \begin{aligned} &\text{Input } G, c, s, t\\ &f \equiv 0\\ &\text{while there is an augmenting path } P \text{ in the auxiliary graph } G_f:\\ &\quad m = \min_{e' \in P}\{c_f(e')\}\\ &\quad \text{for each } e'=(u,v)\in P:\\ &\qquad \text{if } e' \text{ is a forward edge, increase } f(u,v) \text{ by } m\\ &\qquad \text{else decrease } f(v,u) \text{ by } m\\ &\text{return } f \end{aligned} $$ Define $C = \sum_{e=(s,v)\in E} c(e)$ (the sum of capacities of edges leaving the source), then we make the claim that: When $\sum_{e=(s,v)\in E} c(e) \leq C$, the FF algo. terminates after at most $C$ iterations of the "while" loop in L2. ## Cuts in Graphs **Definition: $s-t$ cut** A $s-t$ cut is a partition of $V$ into two sets $A, B$ such that $s \in A$ and $t \in B$. **Definition: Capacity** The capacity of $(A, B)$ is $c(A, B) = \sum_{\text{e outgoing from A}}c(e)$ ### Min-cut-max-flow **Proposition** Let $(G,c,s,t)$ be a flow network, and let $f^{FF}$ be the flow returned by the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm. Then, there is an $s-t$ cut $(A,B)$ such that $⊽(f^{FF}) = c(A,B)$ **Fact** For every flow network $(G,c,s,t)$ and flow $f$ and $s-t$ cut $(A, B)$, - $⊽(f) = \sum_{\text{e from A to B}}f(e) - \sum_{\text{e from B to A}}f(e)$ In particular, $⊽(f) \leq c(A, B)$. We will prove this: $$⊽(f) = \sum_{\text{e from A to B}}f(e) - \sum_{\text{e from B to A}}f(e)$$ $$\leq \sum_{\text{e from A to B}}f(e) = c(A, B)$$ ### Attempt 2 of FF: Bucketing Implementation - Start with augmenting paths that have a large capacity - Let $G_f(w) =$ residual graph, removing edges with $c(e) < w$ - Augment via $G_f(C)$, then $G_f(C / 2)$ then $G_f(C / 4)$ etc. $$ \begin{aligned} \textbf{Input: } & G, c, s, t \\[4pt] 1.\;& f \equiv 0,\quad w = \sum_{\text{e outgoing from s}}{c(e)} \\[6pt] 2.\;& \textbf{while } w \ge 1: \\ 3.\;& \quad \textbf{while there exists an augmenting path } P \text{ in } G_f^{(w)}: \\ 4.\;& \qquad \text{augment } f \text{ by } P \\ 5.\;& \quad w \leftarrow \frac{w}{2} \\ 6.\;& \textbf{return } f \end{aligned} $$ Has **TC**: $O( \log(|C|) ⋅ |E|^2 )$ #### Lemma After each iteration of the "while" loop, using value $w$ and yielding a flow $f$, there is an $s-t$ cut $(A, B)$, with capacity at most $⊽(f) + |E| \cdot w$ ##### Proof Define $A =\{ \text{vertices reachable from s in } G_f(w) \}$ and $B = V \backslash A$ WTS $c(A,B) = \sum_{\text{e outgoing from A}}c(e) \leq ⊽(f) + |E| \cdot w$ After an iteration of the "while" loop, there are no more augmenting paths $P$ in $G_f(w)$ that have capacity at least $w$. This means that there are no simple $s - t$ paths that have a bottleneck gte. $w$, by definition. Thus the capacity of the edges outgoing from A can be no larger than $w$. #### Corollary At each iteration of the "while" loop there are at most $2 \dot |E|$ flow augmentation steps. ### Attempt 3: Edmonds-Karp Implementation of FF **Input $G, c, s, t$** $$ \begin{aligned} 1.\ &\text{let } f \equiv 0 \\ 2.\ &\text{while BFS on } G_f \text{ finds a shortest augmenting path } P: \\ 3.\ &\quad m = \min_{e' \in P} \{ c_f(e') \} \\ 4.\ &\quad \text{for each } e' = (u,v) \in P: \\ 5.\ &\qquad \text{if } e' \text{ is a forward edge increase } f(u,v) \text{ by } m \\ 6.\ &\qquad \text{else decrease } f(v,u) \text{ by } m \\ 7.\ &\text{return } f \end{aligned} $$ Has **TC: $O(|V||E^2|)$** ## Applications of Max Flow ### Finding Minimum Cut Given a flow $f$, we start by building the **residual graph** $G_f$ corresponding to the maximum flow f. For every edge $(u,v)$: - residual capacity forward: $c(u,v) - f(u,v)$ - residual capacity backward: $f(u,v)$ Run BFS from $s$. The edges reachable from $s$ correspond to $A$. $B = V \backslash A$. The minimum cut is the set of edges: $$\{ (u,v) \in E \mid u \in S, v \in T \}$$ This has TC: $O(V + E)$ ### Bipartite Matching In a bipartite graph $G = (V = L \cup R, E)$ a **matching** $M \subseteq E$ is a set of edges such that no two edges touch the same vertex. A matching is perfect if $|M| = \min \{ |L|, |R| \}$ **Input**: A undirected bipartite graph $G = (V = L \cup R, E)$. **Output**: A matching $M \subseteq E$ such that $|M| = m^*$ where $m^* = \max_{\text{ matching } M' \subseteq E} \{ |M'| \}$ We can transform this into a flow / network problem. Given $G$, create $(G',c,s,t)$ by: Let $E' = E$. 1. Directing the edges from $L$ to $R$ in $E'$ 2. Adding the node $s$. Add edges $(s, l), \forall l \in L$ to $E'$. 3. Adding the node $t$. Add edges $(r, t), \forall r \in R$ to $E'$. 4. Define $c(e) = 1, \forall e \in E'$ #### Claim **There is a flow of value $k$ in $G'$ iff. there is a matching in $G$ with $k$ edges.** **$\rightarrow$** Suppose there is a flow of value $k$ in $G$. Let $f$ be this flow. We have $f^{out}(s) = f^{in}(t) = k$ So $k$ edges outgoing from $s$ and incoming to $t$ are saturated since each edge has capacity 1. To show that we have a matching of size $k$, add every edge $(u, v), u \neq s \land v \neq t$ to the set $M$. This set has $|M| = k$ because # Textbook ## Chapter 7.7 Extensions to Max Flow ### Problem 1: Circulation with Demands - Instead of a single $s$ & $t$, what if we had a set of $S$ sources generating flow and a set of $T$ sinks absorbing this flow. - Instead of maximizing flow, imagine sources have fixed supply values and sinks have fixed demand values and our goal is ship flow from nodes with supply to those with demand. - "Satisfy the demand with the available supply" #### Setup - Given a flow network $G = (V, E)$ with capacities on the edges. - For each node $v \in V$ is a demand $d_v$. - If $d_v > 0$, this indicates that the node $v$ has a demand of $d_v$ for flow. - Meaning that the node is a sink, and it wishes to receive du units more flow than it sends out. - If $d_v < 0$, this indicates that $v$ has a supply of $-d_v$ - The node is a source, and it wishes to send out $-d_v$ units more flow than it receives. - If $d_v = 0$, then the node $v$ is neither a source nor a sink. We will assume that all capacities and demands are integers. We use $S$ to denote the set of all nodes with negative demand and $T$ to denote the set of all nodes with positive demand. We say that a circulation with demands $\{ d_v \}$ is a function $f$ that assigns a non-negative real number to each edge and satisfies the following two conditions: 1. **Capacity conditions:** For each $e \in E$, we have $0 \leq f(e) \leq c_e$. 2. **Demand conditions:** For each $v \in V$, we have $v$, $f^{in}(v) - f^{out}(v) = d_v$ ### Building Up **Theorem 7.49** If there exists a feasible circulation with demands $\{ d_v \}$, then $\sum_v d_v = 0$. - Suppose there exists a feasible circulation with demands $\{ d_v \}$. - So $\sum_v d_v = \sum_v f^{in}(v) - f^{out}(v)$ - Consider the value $f(e)$ for each edge $e = (u, v)$. It is counted exactly twice: - Once in $f^{out}(u)$ and once in $f^{in}(v)$ - Since this happens for each edge, they cancel out. From **7.49**, we know that: $$\sum_{v:d_v > 0}d_v = \sum_{v:d_v < 0}-d_v$$ Let $D$ denote this common value. ### Algo. #### Idea Attach a "super-source" $s*$ to each node in $S$, and a "super-sink" $t*$ to each node in $T$. To be specific: 1. Create a graph $G'$ from $G$ by adding new nodes $s*$ and $t*$ to $G$. 2. For each node $v \in T$ (each node $v$ with $d_v > 0$) we add an edge $(v, t*)$ with capacity $d_v$. 3. For each node $u \in S$ (each node with $d_v< 0$) we add an edge $(s*, u)$ with capacity $-d_v$. We carry the remaining structure of $G$ over to $G’$ unchanged. ## Notes - A lot of important results and problems stem from finding a min-cut
